title: Deque conjecture
formal: Start from an arbitrary binary search tree containing $n$ ordered keys, and perform $m$ legal double-ended queue operations. Insert-min creates a new minimum as the root with the old tree as its right child; insert-max is symmetric. Delete-min splays the minimum to the root, removes it, and keeps its right subtree; delete-max is symmetric. Is the total number of primitive pointer operations and rotations always $O(n+m)$, with a universal constant? This is Tarjan’s deque conjecture for the specified splay implementation.
why: I include this because it tests whether one general-purpose adaptive representation can recognize a workload whose optimal cost is linear. The remaining gap is tiny numerically but significant mathematically: a proof would explain why expensive local restructuring cannot accumulate across arbitrary alternations of the two ends.
definitions: Splaying uses the standard zig, zig-zig, and zig-zag rules. Deletions are allowed only on a nonempty tree, and an inserted key must be outside the current key range at the specified end. Amortized cost is a bound on the total sequence, not a worst-case guarantee for each deletion. The initial tree may have any shape.

progress.text: Pettie proves $O((n+m)\alpha^*(n+m))$ total cost, where $\alpha^*$ counts how many iterations of the inverse-Ackermann function reduce the argument to a constant.
Levy and Tarjan connect the deque conjecture to a subsequence property sufficient for dynamic optimality. This provides a structural route to a proof, not the required linear bound itself.
The new analysis of splay competitiveness still describes the deque guarantee as nearly constant per operation. Its general search bound does not supply constant amortized deque cost.

status_note: Reviewed 10 September 2026, including the July 2026 splay result. The conjecture asks for linear total cost under insertions and deletions at either end.

context_blocks.text: A deque allows insertion and deletion at either end of a sequence. A linked representation can implement this abstract interface in constant time per operation. The conjecture concerns what happens when the same interface is implemented by a self-adjusting search tree: it asks whether the tree automatically achieves the linear total cost available for this restricted workload.

Deleting the minimum of a long left spine can require many rotations in a single operation. That does not disprove the conjecture, because the initial tree contributes an additive budget proportional to its size. The real difficulty is to understand whether alternating insertions and deletions at opposite ends can repeatedly rebuild expensive configurations.

For a concrete contrast, deleting keys in increasing order is a sequential-access pattern. A deque workload can switch ends after every operation and introduce new extreme keys between deletions. A bound for one monotone scan therefore does not immediately control this more flexible sequence.

The known total bound has an iterated inverse-Ackermann factor, which grows extraordinarily slowly but is asymptotically unbounded. Removing it would answer a structural question about how rotations reuse earlier work. This is a focused subproblem of the broader study of splaying, with updates included explicitly rather than only searches.

review_note: Individually written from the cited primary sources. The importance assessment is editorial. New preprint proofs have not been independently verified.
answer_criterion: Prove a universal \(O(n+m)\) total bound for the specified splay implementation, or prove that the ratio between total cost and \(n+m\) is unbounded over legal initial trees and operation sequences.

importance.reason: A longstanding concrete stress test for splay-tree adaptivity, already on the elementary deque interface; less sweeping than dynamic optimality.

sentences: A deque permits insertions and deletions at either end of an ordered collection.
This question studies the implementation that inserts extreme keys and splays an extreme key before deleting it.
It asks whether every operation sequence costs linear total time, including an allowance for the initial tree.
Alternating ends and inserting new keys creates behavior beyond a single sorted scan.
The conjecture would show that self-adjusting search trees automatically attain the efficiency expected from this restricted interface.
